content.text: Clanker’s current code explicitly disables payments, which explains those replies. Kernel now has a separate payment integration, so the path is to connect that to Clanker with purchase approval through Slack. I’m checking whether it supports the checkout used by Zepto.

**The solution is to give Clanker a payment tool that completes purchases you approve through Slack.**

The current block comes from our implementation: Clanker’s policy says payment is owner-only, and its payment handlers are disabled. The old card executor was removed during the Kernel migration. Sending you back to the sign-in link was also a broken checkout handoff. [Current policy](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/clanker_policy.py:4), [disabled handlers](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/runtime/vault/payments.py:5).

Kernel **does support payments**, including protected card filling and wallet integrations. Clanker needs to integrate that capability. [Kernel payment documentation](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/payments).

The flow I recommend is:

1. **Clanker prepares checkout** and shows the verified merchant, items, delivery details and final total in Slack.
2. **You approve that exact purchase**, for example “Pay ₹69.” Approval belongs to your account and that checkout; changed totals require fresh approval.
3. **Clanker completes checkout** through Kernel’s payment integration. Card enrollment and any required bank authentication use a secure private link opened from Slack. You don’t operate Clanker’s browser.
4. **Clanker verifies the merchant’s order record** and returns the confirmation. An uncertain result triggers reconciliation before another payment attempt.

**For your India use case, I’d evaluate Kernel + AgentCard first.** It uses placeholder card values while the real card stays outside the agent’s browser, and Kernel documents support for specific Razorpay checkout requests. Kernel’s Link integration currently requires a US phone number. [AgentCard integration](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/integrations/wallets/agentcard), [Link requirements](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/integrations/wallets/stripe-link).

So saving a card alone won’t fix this. We need the wallet integration, purchase approval, payment execution and order verification together. The same approval flow can support COD when the merchant offers it.

**The remaining unknown is whether Zepto’s actual checkout matches a supported payment flow. That needs verification before promising it will work there.**

Banks may still require OTP or 3DS authentication, and individual merchant checkouts need verification.

**The Slack experience is feasible now. Optional card retention is the specific provider capability still to validate.**

Kernel’s native provider enrolls your card and creates payment tokens for purchases. I’ll check how it handles card details, approvals, issuer eligibility and the ₹500 limit in the current API.

**Kernel’s native provider lets an agent pay with your existing card using network tokens.** Its API identifier is `provider: "kernel"`.

Here’s the flow:

1. **Enroll your card privately.** A Kernel-hosted page collects your card and email. A `wallet` item represents that enrolled card. Kernel’s documentation says the original card number never reaches Kernel; the underlying storage partner isn’t named. [Wallet specification](https://github.com/kernel/kernel-python-sdk/blob/main/src/kernel/types/vaults/kernel_wallet_vault_item_spec.py)

2. **Prepare a purchase.** Clanker creates a `card` item containing the amount, currency and merchant checkout URL. Kernel obtains a replacement card number, expiry and one-time three-digit code, stored encrypted for checkout. [Card specification](https://github.com/kernel/kernel-python-sdk/blob/main/src/kernel/types/vaults/kernel_card_vault_item_spec.py)

3. **Approve it.** Visa requires a hosted approval using a Visa passkey. Mastercard requires no additional hosted approval in this integration. Clanker would still require your approval through the **Pay ₹X** flow. [API specification](https://api.onkernel.com/spec.json)

4. **Complete checkout.** Kernel fills the payment fields only on the configured merchant origin. Clanker submits checkout and checks the merchant’s order confirmation. Kernel itself doesn’t establish whether the merchant charged the card. [Payment state](https://github.com/kernel/kernel-python-sdk/blob/main/src/kernel/types/vaults/kernel_card_state.py)

For **Remember this card**, we retain the wallet. For **Use once**, we could remove the wallet and enrolled card after resolving the payment outcome. That involves temporary enrollment; there’s no documented native retention checkbox. [Deletion behavior](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/api-reference/vaults/delete-a-vault-item-and-invalidate-its-secret-value)

Two significant limits:

- **Issuer eligibility:** your bank must support the required network token. Supporting INR doesn’t establish support for your particular Indian card.
- **Published amount cap:** 50,000 minor units, which means **₹500 per INR purchase**. [Live schema](https://api.onkernel.com/spec.json)

Also, the payment token enters the browser during filling and can be read through unrestricted browser access, so Clanker must protect those observations. [Fill documentation](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/vaults/fill)

**The API and official SDK confirm this integration exists. Your card’s eligibility and Zepto compatibility remain untested.**

**Evervault Browser Tokens is the closest alternative I found.** Its docs explicitly support Kernel and using existing cards at third-party checkouts. [Provider docs](https://docs.evervault.com/browser-tokens)

We could build your flow like this:

1. **Slack: “Pay ₹69”** → opens our secure page with Evervault’s embedded card form.
2. User enters their card and presses **Pay**. The form returns encrypted details to our backend. [Card collection](https://docs.evervault.com/cards/card-collection)
3. Clanker fills temporary card aliases into the merchant checkout. Evervault substitutes the real details only when sending them to approved payment hosts. Clanker completes checkout and verifies the order. [How it works](https://docs.evervault.com/browser-tokens)

There are three material catches:

- **Access and cost:** Browser Tokens is in preview and requires provider access. Evervault publishes **$995/month plus usage** for its platform; Browser Tokens pricing/inclusion needs confirmation. [Pricing](https://evervault.com/pricing)
- **Bank verification:** OTP/3DS challenges can still require the user. This provider doesn’t eliminate them. [Limitations](https://docs.evervault.com/browser-tokens)
- **Remembering cards:** For Indian cards, we must verify the approach against RBI’s card-storage restrictions. Encryption alone doesn’t establish compliance. CVV also cannot be retained after authorization, so subsequent payments may require it again. [RBI](https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/BS_CircularIndexDisplay.aspx?Id=12159), [PCI](https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/faqs/are-merchants-allowed-to-request-card-verification-codes-values-from-cardholders/)

**This is a credible route for “enter card → we handle checkout.” Zepto compatibility and Indian saved-card support remain unverified.**

**“Browser egress” means the network request leaving the browser for the merchant or payment processor.**

In the flow described here:

1. Clanker fills **placeholder card values**, called aliases, into checkout and clicks Pay.
2. The outgoing payment request passes through Kernel, which checks its authorization.
3. Kernel either substitutes an approved payment credential or lets the connected provider execute the request, then returns the result to the browser.

That keeps the actual card number and CVV out of Clanker’s context, screenshots and browser. Clanker still navigates checkout and checks the order confirmation. [Article](https://www.kernel.sh/blog/agentic-payments)

**There’s a distinction for our chosen setup:** this article describes **Link and AgentCard**. Kernel’s native `provider: "kernel"` explicitly **doesn’t use aliases or egress substitution**. It fills a network token number and one-time code into checkout instead, keeping the original card number out of the browser. [Native card contract](https://github.com/kernel/kernel-python-sdk/blob/main/src/kernel/types/vaults/kernel_card_state.py)

**The design is: Kernel enrolls the card and supplies payment credentials; Clanker handles checkout and confirms the order. Both items use `provider: "kernel"`.**

1. **Show “Pay ₹X” in Slack.**  
   Clanker prepares the cart. Our backend verifies the merchant, items, total and currency. Clicking Pay opens an authenticated private payment page tied to that user and purchase.

2. **Connect the card when needed.**  
   We create a `wallet` item and redirect the user to Kernel’s returned `card_enrollment` page. It collects **card details plus email**. After enrollment, we check both `connected` status and payment-method eligibility; being stored doesn’t guarantee the card can pay. [Wallet contract](https://github.com/kernel/kernel-python-sdk/blob/main/src/kernel/types/vaults/kernel_wallet_vault_item_spec.py)

3. **Authorize this purchase.**  
   We create a fresh `card` item referencing that wallet, with the verified merchant, amount and currency, then invoke its advertised `authorize` operation. **Visa requires a Visa passkey approval; Mastercard requires no additional hosted purchase approval.** Bank authentication may still apply. [Purchase contract](https://github.com/kernel/kernel-python-sdk/blob/main/src/kernel/types/vaults/kernel_card_vault_item_spec.py)

4. **Fill and submit checkout.**  
   The browser must have the vault attached. Once the card is `ready`, Kernel’s `fill` operation writes a **network token number, expiry and one-time code** into the merchant’s fields. Clanker submits checkout and pauses for private bank verification if required. The original card number stays outside the browser; the payment token enters it. [Fill contract](https://github.com/kernel/kernel-python-sdk/blob/main/src/kernel/types/vaults/fill_vault_item_operation_request_param.py)

5. **Verify and report the result.**  
   Clanker checks the merchant’s actual order record before saying “Paid” or “Order placed” in Slack. Kernel doesn’t observe the merchant charge. An uncertain submission must be reconciled before another attempt. [Payment verification](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/payments)

For the ₹69 example, the purchase item would contain:

```json
{
  "type": "card",
  "spec": {
    "provider": "kernel",
    "wallet": "user-card",
    "merchant_name": "Example merchant",
    "merchant_url": "https://merchant.example/checkout",
    "merchant_country": "IN",
    "amount": 6900,
    "currency": "inr"
  }
}
```

**“Remember card” is a preference we implement on our private payment page.**

- **Checked:** retain the connected wallet for future purchases.
- **Unchecked:** temporarily enroll the card, reconcile the purchase, then delete that wallet to remove the enrolled card. Removal can remain pending if an operation is unresolved or deletion fails. We only report “card removed” after deletion succeeds. [Deletion contract](https://kernel.sh/docs/api-reference/vaults/delete-a-vault-item-and-invalidate-its-secret-value)

Kernel doesn’t document a native `remember=false` option or custom checkbox inside its hosted enrollment form. [Live API schema](https://www.kernel.sh/openapi.json)

**Current limits:** the published INR maximum is **₹500 per purchase**, issuer eligibility is required, and merchant acceptance isn’t universal. Those limits come from the [native purchase contract](https://github.com/kernel/kernel-python-sdk/blob/main/src/kernel/types/vaults/kernel_card_vault_item_spec.py).

**Verified so far:** the public API contract. Our project’s access, your card’s eligibility and a successful Zepto payment remain untested; this flow is not implemented in Clanker yet.
